**AI coding research brief — October 30, 2026**

Four new papers from October 23–30, ranked for their practical relevance to Quadratus. These are fresh preprints; the experiments below are proposed applications, not demonstrated improvements in this repository.

**1. Skeleton Coding: Program Structure as a Specification for Agents**  
October 28, 2026 · [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38214)

Across four models and three benchmarks, the best structural specifications—function stubs, types and contracts—reduced mean test error from 40.7% to 21.0% relative to the best end-to-end behavioral specifications, a 48.4% relative reduction.

**Why read it:** It makes delegation boundaries concrete: workers receive a shared structure as well as expected behavior. The important limitation is that specifications were derived from existing reference implementations, then used to reconstruct programs. This does not establish that a master agent can invent equally good skeletons for new requirements, or that authoring them pays for itself.

**Quadratus experiment:** Have the coordinator define minimal interfaces, ownership and local contracts before delegating. Compare against prose task descriptions using identical acceptance tests and total budgets, including specification creation. Measure hidden-test success, integration defects and rework.

**2. Evolving Agent Teams**  
October 27, 2026 · [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36848)

A supervisor diagnoses stalled progress and reorganizes worker roles, using persistent learning records and team history. In a matched $800 inference-budget comparison on MLA decode, its two runs reached 0.721× and 0.685× production FlashInfer performance, versus 0.602×/0.598× for K-Search. A separate extended-budget run reached about 1.2× and beat FlashInfer on 36 of 47 workloads.

**Why read it:** It supplies a concrete mechanism for changing the team when its current approach stops working. The matched-budget results still trail production FlashInfer; the headline speedup required more budget. Most comparisons use only two runs, and GPU optimization does not establish gains on ordinary repository repairs.

**Quadratus experiment:** After a defined number of unsuccessful iterations, permit one bounded role change—for example, an independent challenger or knowledge integrator. Compare against a fixed team with the same total budget and correctness checks. Record recovery rate, regressions and coordination cost.

**3. MUSE: Multi-Level Memory with Selective Runtime Injection for Scientific Coding Agents**  
October 28, 2026 · [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38332)

MUSE separates global guidance, task-level approaches and implementation lessons. During execution, retrieval uses current actions and tool results; an LLM gate supplies one relevant lesson with a concrete check, or supplies nothing. On 84 SWE-bench Science test tasks, pass rate reached 40.5%, versus 35.7% for the strongest memory baseline and 29.8% without memory.

**Why read it:** This turns shared memory into timely, actionable advice. Memory was frozen before testing on held-out problems, and comparisons shared the same historical trajectories. However, the study uses one model backbone, the repository-repair sample is small, and the reported pass rates do not establish a net cost or latency advantage.

**Quadratus experiment:** Compare initialization-only retrieval against selective retrieval after failed tests or suspicious tool results. Require each injected lesson to identify its evidence, applicability conditions and next check. Count gate calls and memory preparation in total cost.

**4. Repairs for Whom? Evaluator–Executor Mismatch in Selecting Repairs for Failed LLM Agents**  
October 28, 2026 · [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38610)

Holding failed trajectories and candidate interventions fixed, the authors find that a stronger model can choose worse recovery actions for a weaker executor. At equal rollout budgets, selecting for Qwen2.5-7B using Qwen2.5-14B reduced expected net gain by 0.25 in ALFWorld and 0.07 in WebShop relative to selection using the executor's own rollouts.

**Why read it:** A master agent's preferred recovery may rely on capabilities the assigned worker lacks. These are single-step action repairs in restorable text environments, with two small deployed models—not code-patch evaluations. Transfer to coding coordination remains a hypothesis.

**Quadratus experiment:** On archived failed tasks, let a stronger coordinator propose recovery plans, then compare coordinator-only selection with brief continuations by the actual assigned worker. Label stored recovery outcomes with executor model and harness configuration; measure verified completion per total token.

**The single most promising idea to try**

**Specify delegation interfaces before workers start.** On a small held-out set of multi-file tasks, compare current delegation with a coordinator-authored skeleton of interfaces, responsibilities and local contracts. Keep acceptance tests and total budgets fixed, count planning overhead, and measure integration defects alongside final success. This directly tests whether clearer task boundaries improve the master-agent workflow.
